tldr: The authors propose Kirin, a framework that accurately reconstructs smooth 3D skeletal motion from monocular in-the-wild videos to build a large-scale dataset called AiM3D, and generates realistic motions and 3D animations for diverse quadrupeds conditioned on both text and images.
hero_caption: The overall architecture of Kirin. The left side shows the pipeline taking text and an image as input to generate 3D motion via a diffusion model, while automatically skinning and animating a 3D mesh generated from the image. The right side illustrates the structure that integrates text, image, and timestep information using DistilBERT and DINOv3, denoising and generating motion with a Transformer decoder.
overview:
Modeling animal motion is essential not only for understanding biology and ecology, but also for motion design in quadruped robotics and CG animation. However, collecting precise motion data in capture studios like we do for humans is difficult. Researchers have had to rely on small-scale, artist-crafted CG animations.

The authors realized that they could directly learn 3D motion from the massive number of wild animal videos on the web. By combining an optimization pipeline that temporally smooths monocular 3D pose estimates with 3D point tracking, they built AiM3D, the first large-scale dataset pairing high-quality 3D motion and text captions from about 30,000 videos.

Because quadrupeds have vastly different kinematics depending on species and body shape, the authors developed a diffusion-based motion generation model that conditions on both text prompts and reference image features. The generated skeletal motion is then automatically rigged onto a 3D mesh created from a single image, animating it without artifacts.

Experiments showed that the proposed method outperforms prior work in motion fidelity and text alignment on both an in-house test set and an unseen external dataset (AnimalML3D). Compared to existing animation methods based on video generation models, Kirin produces stable, natural 3D quadruped animations without structural collapses or shrinking bodies.
contributions: Developed a method to accurately and smoothly reconstruct motion by separating local pose and global translation from monocular videos, creating AiM3D, a large-scale dataset aligning about 30,000 quadruped animal videos, texts, and 3D motions.
Proposed the first animal motion diffusion model conditioned on both text and images to capture the kinematic constraints of different animal species and body shapes.

Built an end-to-end system that automatically generates render-ready 4D animal animations from a single image and text by combining single-image 3D mesh generation, automatic rigging, and linear blend skinning.
Demonstrated superior performance over existing state-of-the-art methods in motion quality, diversity, and text alignment on both the proposed dataset and an unseen external test set (AnimalML3D).

sections.heading: Can we learn animal motion directly from wild videos?
sections.summary: Unlike human motion, animal motion is tough to record in a studio, making data scarcity the biggest bottleneck. This work introduces Kirin, a system that extracts smooth 3D skeletal motions from web videos and generates diverse animal motions conditioned on both text and images.
sections.details:
Human 3D motion research has advanced rapidly thanks to motion capture technology and large-scale datasets. For animals, however, high-quality data is severely lacking because we cannot simply bring wild animals into a laboratory.

Past work relied on artist-animated CG assets or game datasets. These covered only limited actions like walking or feeding, missing the dynamic and diverse behaviors of wild animals. Meanwhile, the internet is full of diverse animal videos. The starting point of this research was to see if we could learn motion directly from these videos by combining recent monocular 3D reconstruction techniques with vision-language models (VLMs).

In Kirin, the authors take an existing animal video collection (AiM) and accurately estimate and smooth both local joint rotations and global translations in camera space. This produced AiM3D, a dataset with about 30,000 motions and 180,000 captions. They then built a motion diffusion model conditioned on text and images, completing a pipeline that automatically rigs and animates the generated skeletal motion onto a 3D mesh derived from an image.

sections.heading: Where animal motion reconstruction and generation stand today
sections.summary: This section reviews animal motion data collection, 3D animal reconstruction from monocular inputs, and motion generation models. Kirin stands out by establishing the first large-scale multimodal foundation with aligned video, text, and 3D motion across multiple species.
sections.details:
### Evolution of Animal Motion Datasets
Conventional animal datasets were limited to a few species captured in lab environments or relied on artist-made CG data. Some tried estimating poses from video, but they had very few sequences (such as 11 in BADJA) or very short clips of around 15 frames (APT-36K). AiM collected around 30,000 videos across 23 species, but lacked 3D motion labels. This study builds on AiM by adding 3D motion and captions, turning it into a complete multimodal dataset.

### Trends in 3D Animal Reconstruction
Monocular 3D animal reconstruction approaches are split between parametric model-based methods (like SMAL) and model-free methods (like MagicPony). Model-free methods are flexible, but they lack an explicit articulated skeleton, making them unsuitable for generating joint motion. This study initializes poses using AniMer, which is based on the 35-joint SMAL model, and optimizes across entire sequences to preserve natural 3D geometry while eliminating temporal jitter.

### Positioning Animal Motion Generation
In motion generation, methods like OmniMotionGPT transfer human motion knowledge, while AniMo trains on synthetic data extracted from games. Among real-video approaches, Ponymation exists only for horse videos and is limited to single-species, unconditional generation. Kirin covers 23 quadruped categories and is the first animal motion generation framework to use both text and image conditioning.

sections.heading: Precise video reconstruction, image-guided diffusion, and auto-rigging
sections.summary: Kirin's core pipeline consists of three stages: extracting joint poses and global translation separately from web videos, denoising motion in latent space conditioned on combined text and image features, and transferring skinning weights onto an image-derived 3D mesh for animation.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Extracting 3D Motion from Web Videos
To robustly reconstruct animal movement from video, the method decouples local joint pose estimation from global camera-space translation. This allows the system to capture fine joint movements without being confused by camera shake or subject displacement.

- **Initialization and Optimization**: For each frame, segmentation masks and 2D keypoints are extracted. AniMer provides initial SMAL parameters (shape coefficients $ oldsymbol{ eta} \in \mathbb{R}^{41}$ and 35 joint rotation angles $ oldsymbol{	heta} \in \mathbb{R}^{35 	imes 3}$). The pipeline then optimizes a sequence-shared shape $ oldsymbol{ eta}$ alongside 6D rotation representations $\mathbf{r}_t$ per frame. By balancing a keypoint projection loss $\lambda_{	ext{data}}$ with a geodesic rotation smoothness term $\lambda_{	ext{smooth}}$ across frames, it reconstructs flicker-free trajectories in under one second per frame.
- **Global Translation Recovery**: A 3D point tracking model (SpatialTrackerV2) extracts the full trajectory from the original video. Its head-to-tail scale ratio is matched and fused with the SMAL skeleton.
- **Caption Generation**: Gemini 2.5 Flash is used with six distinct prompts per video to generate detailed, diverse motion descriptions, yielding about 180,000 captions in total.

### 3.2 Image-Conditioned Motion Diffusion Model
For quadrupeds, a text prompt like "a dog is trotting" cannot distinguish between a short-legged corgi and a long-legged greyhound, leaving kinematic constraints ambiguous. To solve this, the authors introduced image conditioning to directly specify appearance and build.

- **Architecture**: Based on MDM (Motion Diffusion Model), text is encoded with DistilBERT and images with a pretrained DINOv3. The text features $\mathbf{z}_{	ext{text}}$, image features $\mathbf{z}_{	ext{img}}$, and timestep embedding $\mathbf{z}_t$ are linearly projected and summed, then fed into cross-attention layers across each Transformer decoder block.
- **Training and Inference**: Using Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) where each modality is independently dropped with 20% probability, the model supports flexible control during inference using text only, image only, or both together.

### 3.3 Automatic Rigging and Animation of Generated Assets
A single-image 3D generation model (Rodin) reconstructs a T-pose 3D mesh from the input image. An optimization step fits the SMAL template's position and joint rotations to this mesh to determine the bind pose. Next, $k$-nearest neighbors ($k=10$) transfers the SMAL skinning weights to each vertex of the 3D mesh. Applying Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) yields a 3D asset that deforms naturally according to the generated skeletal motion.

captions.F10: The 3D motion reconstruction pipeline. From the input video, initial local 3D skeleton poses are estimated and temporally smoothed, while global translation is tracked separately with a 3D tracker. Both are then scaled and merged.

sections.heading: Higher motion fidelity and artifact-free mesh animations
sections.summary: Both quantitative and qualitative evaluations were conducted for motion generation and reconstruction. The proposed method significantly outperforms existing baselines like AniMo and Puppeteer across text alignment and naturalness metrics, with ablations confirming the power of image conditioning.
sections.details:
### Quantitative Evaluation of Motion Generation
The evaluation uses the AiM3D test split (230 sequences) and an unseen external dataset, AnimalML3D (1,260 artist-crafted motions). Metrics include R-Precision and MM-Dist for text-motion alignment, alongside FID and Diversity for generation quality.

Compared to the existing animal motion generator AniMo on the AiM3D test set, Kirin outperformed AniMo even with text input alone. Adding image conditioning dramatically improved FID, moving generation closest to the real motion distribution. Furthermore, on the unseen AnimalML3D dataset, Kirin achieved the best scores across all metrics, proving the strong generalization of priors learned from web videos.

### Qualitative Comparisons and Failure Modes
In skeletal comparisons, AniMo produced a lying-down motion when asked to "rear up," and cat skeletons severely shrank or collapsed over time. In contrast, Kirin preserved consistent body proportions while faithfully executing turning or rearing actions as instructed.

When compared with Puppeteer, an animation method that deforms meshes via video generation models, video inconsistencies often caused the animal to remain nearly stationary or deform unnaturally. Kirin directly applies physically smooth 3D trajectories extracted from real videos to skinning, achieving dynamic, artifact-free motions.

### Ablation on Image Conditioning
Adding image conditioning significantly improved fidelity and alignment metrics like FID and R-Precision. The reference image imposes strong spatial constraints on limb lengths and body proportions. However, these tighter constraints slightly reduced diversity, revealing a natural trade-off.

sections.heading: How video-driven approaches open up the future of animal motion
sections.summary: Kirin establishes an end-to-end framework that extracts and learns 3D motion from in-the-wild videos, generating high-quality animal animations from text and images. This provides a new foundation for quadruped robotics, biomechanics, and digital entertainment.
sections.details: This paper presented AiM3D, a large-scale dataset constructed by recovering high-quality 3D motions from in-the-wild animal videos, and proposed a new diffusion generation model conditioned on both text and images. By combining automatic rigging for image-generated 3D assets, the authors built a complete system capable of producing render-ready 4D animal assets from a single image and prompt.\n\nThis approach opens a scalable path for animal motion modeling—where studio capture is impractical—by tapping into the vast resource of web videos. It is expected to support a wide range of downstream applications, including adaptive trajectory generation for quadruped robots and behavioral analysis in biology.

sections.heading: Dataset details, global translation, and the impact of image conditioning
sections.summary: The appendix provides details on the AiM3D dataset composition, human quality verification, visualizations of global translation, and demonstrations of how skeleton proportions and gaits adapt to different input images for the same text prompt.
sections.details:
### Dataset Scale and Human Quality Evaluation
AiM3D contains 29,979 motion sequences across 23 quadruped categories, split into 230 test sequences and 29,749 training sequences. In a manual visual check of 100 randomly sampled test sequences, 86% of the reconstructed motions were judged satisfactory, free of unnatural distortions or jitter. Most failures occurred when legs were completely occluded from top-down or front angles. Furthermore, the VLM-generated captions scored an average of 4.62 out of 5, with 90% judged to be accurate, error-free descriptions.

### Gait Differences Induced by Image Conditioning
As shown in Figure F12, even with the identical prompt "An animal is walking," providing different reference images (such as a bear, raccoon, dog, or horse) clearly alters both skeletal proportions and species-appropriate leg stepping (gait). This visually verifies that image features serve as effective morphological context.

captions.F6: Visualization of global translation trajectories in reconstructed motions. Red arrows projected on the ground show the path of the root joint, demonstrating that the system accurately tracks dynamic straight and turning movements through space.
captions.F12: Effect of image conditioning. Given the identical prompt 'An animal is walking', skeletal proportions and footfall patterns (gaits) appropriately adapt to the anatomical features of each species based on the input image.

takeaways: Even for difficult-to-capture subjects, high-quality, large-scale motion datasets can be constructed by decoupling and optimizing 3D pose estimation and point-tracked global translation from monocular videos.

When generating motion for subjects with large morphological differences (such as diverse quadrupeds), injecting reference image features alongside text prompts plays a decisive role in enforcing kinematic constraints and improving realism.
Rigging smooth 3D skeletal motions learned from real videos provides much better long-term geometric consistency and physical plausibility than deforming meshes through video generation models.
limitations: Using a single skeletal topology from elephants to rabbits prevents the model from fully handling extreme species-specific anatomical proportions and structural variations.
Tail motion—crucial for emotional expression and balance—is excluded from modeling due to video occlusions and keypoint definition constraints in the original footage.

Physical inconsistencies like foot sliding or floating cannot be completely eliminated due to monocular depth ambiguities and occlusions, and the framework does not yet integrate explicit physics simulation or contact constraints.
